turn_text: Well, Alan, actually Woody was the one that came up with the idea initially, and it was not for himself, because for those of you who knew Woody Williams, he dedicated his life to service for our country, for our nation that he loved. And it was his idea to honor the greatest generation of our country and those in particular who tirelessly fought for their country. And he was a medal of honor recipient. But he never had plans to be the very last one. That's for sure. But he wanted to make sure that we honored the last Medal of Honor recipient in our nation's capital. And so that's why in 2019, I did the resolution. And at that time, there were four remaining recipients. Then there were three. Then there were two. It was Woody. And he always felt like he was part of a team. And he was very vocal about that. And his commitment to his fellow veterans and countrymen really embodies who he was. I also served in, well, I was a member of Rotary with him in Little Tiny Milton, West Virginia for almost 20 years. And when I'd come in for lunch, he'd be sitting back there reading the newspaper just being woody and he was a country boy at heart. He was a very religious man, you know, the older he got the the more the Lord meant to him and he was a servant. So I'm just happy to be the one that initiated everything going on. And I am also thankful to my senators for helping to get it through over the finish line at the end. And the important part that Woody would want everyone to know is that this is for all of our veterans, and we need to continue to help our veterans and to honor them for their service.
